transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doc, it's kind of hard to explain, but I guess it really comes down to what happens after work. I'm a diesel mechanic, you know, working on these massive trucks and buses, and the shifts are just... they're brutal. I mean, ten, sometimes twelve hours, just covered in grease, lifting heavy parts, crawling under rigs. By the time I clock out, my body is aching and my brain is just completely fried. 

So lately, I’ll get off one of these long shifts, and I’ll tell myself on the drive home that I'm just going to grab something small, maybe just have a normal, quiet dinner. But then... I don't know, it just completely snowballs. I'll hit a drive-thru on the way back, and instead of just getting a burger like a normal person, I'll order a massive combo, extra large fries, maybe a couple of extra sandwiches on the side. And you'd think a full fast-food meal would be enough, right? But I get home, and it's like I can't turn the switch off. 

I'll finish all that fast food, and then I immediately start digging through the cupboards for snacks—bags of chips, sleeves of cookies, just tearing through them. Then I'm opening the fridge and just eating whatever leftovers or random stuff I can find in there. Slices of cheese, cold cuts straight out of the package, whatever is sitting on the shelves. It’s just way, way more than I ever planned to eat, and it all happens in just one single sitting. It’s like I get into this zone and I just can't stop myself until it's all gone, and it's been happening so much lately that I just felt like I had to come in and talk to somebody about it.
Do you feel like you're in control of your eating during these episodes?

No, man, not at all. Not even a little bit. That's the scariest part of the whole thing, honestly. It's like... it's like I'm sitting in the passenger seat of my own body, you know? Like I said, I'll be driving home, totally exhausted from wrestling with transmissions and brake lines all day, and I'll have this whole plan in my head. 'Just a burger, man, just one burger.' But then I pull into the drive-thru, and it's like someone else takes over the steering wheel. 

And then when I get home, it gets even worse. Once I start on those nights, it feels like my hands just keep grabbing food on their own. I'll be standing there in the kitchen, still in my dirty work boots, grease under my fingernails, just shoving chips and cookies into my mouth. And the whole time, the whole time, my brain is screaming at me, 'Stop! What are you doing? You're full! You're gonna make yourself sick!' And I *am* feeling sick. My stomach gets so tight and painful, like it's stretched to the absolute limit, like an over-inflated tire that's about to blow. But my hands just keep going. Reaching into the bag, opening the fridge, grabbing more cold cuts, more cheese. I can literally feel how awful it is, how sick I'm getting, and I'm begging myself to just walk away from the kitchen, but I just... I can't. It's like the brakes are completely shot and I'm just rolling downhill, picking up speed, and there's absolutely nothing I can do to stop the crash. It's just a total, complete loss of control.
How often do these episodes of eating out of control happen?

Well, doc, it's... it's a lot, honestly. If I really sit down and think about it, and look back over, say, the last few months, it's been pretty consistent. I'd say most weeks, there's at least one night where it just completely gets away from me like I was describing. Sometimes it's a Tuesday after a particularly rough day dealing with a stubborn transmission, sometimes it's a Friday when I'm just totally burnt out from the whole week. But yeah, most weeks, at least once, I have one of those massive blowouts where I just eat everything in sight. 

But, see, the thing is, it doesn't just end with the eating. That's the other part of this whole mess. After I eat all that food, and my stomach feels like it's going to burst, I just get this overwhelming wave of panic and guilt, you know? It's like, 'Oh man, what did I just do? I can't let all this just sit in my stomach.' So then I have to do something to fix it, to try and undo the damage. Sometimes I end up forcing myself to throw up, which is just... it's awful, I hate doing it, but in the moment it feels like the only way out. Other times I'll take a bunch of laxatives, or I'll just tell myself, 'Right, that's it, you're not eating anything at all tomorrow.' Just totally skip meals the next day to try and balance the scales. Or I'll go to the gym and just punish myself on the treadmill for hours, running until my legs feel like they're going to fall off, just trying to burn it all away. 

And like I said, this cycle—the eating out of control, and then the throwing up, or the laxatives, or the starving, or the crazy workouts—it's been happening at least once a week for several months now. It's like this terrible routine I'm stuck in, and it's exhausting. I mean, working as a diesel mechanic is exhausting enough, but adding all this on top of it? It's just draining the life out of me, doc. It really is.
Do you worry about gaining weight after these episodes of eating?

Yeah, doc, I worry about it constantly. It's like this massive, heavy cloud just hanging over my head all the time, especially after one of those bad nights. I mean, you'd think working the job I do, I'd be burning enough calories wrestling with diesel engines and hauling around heavy tools all day to not have to stress about it so much. But it's... it's an obsession, honestly. 

I'll be getting dressed for work, right? And I'll put on my work pants, the thick canvas ones I wear to the shop, and I can actually feel that they're looser on me. I'll have to pull my belt a notch tighter just to keep them up while I'm crawling under a rig. So, logically, you'd think I'd be like, 'Okay, cool, I'm not gaining weight.' But then I'll step on the scale in the bathroom before I leave, and if that number is up even a single pound—just one pound—my brain just completely short-circuits. 

I instantly feel like I'm getting fat. It doesn't matter how my clothes fit, it doesn't matter how much I sweated at the shop the day before. If the scale goes up even a fraction, I just spiral. I start worrying that I'm going to completely lose control of my whole body, like it's just going to keep expanding and expanding and I won't be able to stop it. It's terrifying, honestly. And it just feeds right back into that whole cycle I was telling you about, making me feel like I have to go to the gym and run myself into the ground, or starve myself the next day just to get that one pound back off. It's just... it's exhausting being so hyper-focused on it all the time, but I just can't seem to turn off that fear.
Do you think your fear of gaining weight is what triggers these episodes of eating out of control?

I honestly... I don't even know, doc. It’s hard to untangle it all, you know? Like, I'm terrified of putting on weight, I really am, like I was just saying, but is that what actually kicks off the whole eating thing? I've sat in my truck for hours after a shift just staring at the steering wheel, trying to figure out why I do this, what actually starts the dominoes falling. 

Sometimes I think, yeah, maybe it is. Maybe I stress so much about that one pound on the scale in the morning that by the time I clock out at the shop, my brain is just completely fried from worrying about it all day while I'm trying to, you know, rebuild a diesel injector or whatever. It takes a lot of focus to do my job, and having that weight panic running in the background all day is exhausting. 

But then... then other times, it doesn't feel like it has anything to do with my weight at all in that specific moment. Like, when I'm pulling into that drive-thru, or when I'm standing in my kitchen tearing through the cabinets, I'm not usually sitting there thinking, 'Oh man, I'm so scared of getting fat, I'm gonna go eat everything.' It’s more like... I don't know, it's just this overwhelming urge, like a pressure valve that just has to pop. I’ll be covered in grease, my back is absolutely aching from being bent over an engine block for nine hours, and my mind is just kind of blank. I'm not thinking about the scale right then. I'm just thinking about the food. 

So, I mean... maybe the fear of the weight is always there in the background, like static on the shop radio that you just can't tune out, but as for it being the actual trigger? The thing that flips the switch and makes me lose control? I really couldn't tell you for sure. It's like... it's like trying to figure out which exact pothole ruined your suspension when you've been driving on a totally washed-out dirt road your whole life, you know what I mean? It's just all a huge, confusing mess up in my head, and I honestly don't know what starts it anymore.
Do you usually feel stressed, anxious, or upset right before these episodes of eating out of control happen?

Man, that's... that's another tough one to pin down. Like, sure, my job is stressful, generally speaking. You try pulling a transmission out of a forty-foot transit bus when the air compressor keeps cutting out and the floor is slick with oil—it's high stress, right? But... right *before* I actually start eating? I really haven't noticed if I'm feeling particularly upset or anxious right at that exact second. 

It's not like I'm sitting there crying or having some kind of panic attack and then decide to go hit the drive-thru. Honestly, half the time my brain is just... blank. Like, I'll be driving home, listening to the radio, maybe just thinking about a manifold I gotta weld the next morning, and I'm not feeling super stressed or anything. I might even be relieved that I'm finally off the clock and heading home. But then I walk through my front door, drop my boots by the mat, and it's just... boom. The urge is just suddenly there. 

It really doesn't seem to matter if I had a smooth day where every bolt came loose like butter, or a nightmare shift where I was busting my knuckles open every five minutes and wanting to yell at the service manager. I've had these blowouts on good days, bad days, boring days... it doesn't seem to discriminate. So, yeah, I really couldn't say if there's a specific emotion or worry tied to it right beforehand. I've tried to pay attention to it, I really have, but it just seems to happen whether I'm in a decent mood, a terrible mood, or just dead tired. It's like the engine just revs up entirely on its own, regardless of who's pushing the pedal, you know? So I really don't think I can say I'm always upset or anxious right before it happens. I just haven't noticed a pattern like that.
Do you ever eat in secret, hiding it from others due to feeling embarrassed or ashamed about what or how much you're eating?

Honestly, doc, no, I don't really hide it. I mean, I don't sneak around or anything. For one thing, I live by myself now in this little duplex over by the interstate, so there's not really anybody around at home to hide it from anyway. It's just me and the TV. But even before that, back when I was splitting rent with my buddy Dave—we went to high school together and then shared this cramped little apartment near the depot for like three years—I never took food into my bedroom or waited for him to fall asleep or anything crazy like that. 

If I was having one of those nights where I just needed to tear through, I don't know, two entire large pizzas and a family-size bag of chips, I’d just sit right there on the living room couch and go at it. Dave would be sitting right next to me playing Xbox, and I'd just be eating. 

And even when I'm out with the guys from the shop, I don't hide how much I'm putting away. You gotta understand, guys in my line of work, we're mostly big dudes with massive appetites anyway. You spend nine, ten hours hauling around one-inch impact wrenches and wrestling with super-single tires that weigh more than a grown man, people just expect you to eat like a horse. So if we all go to the diner after a rough shift and I order three full entrees for myself, nobody bats an eye. They just laugh and tell the waitress I'm fueling the furnace, you know? 

They don't know the half of what's actually going on in my head, obviously, or how much I'm panicking about the calories later, but I don't feel like I have to sneak off to my truck to eat where no one can see me. I just... I just eat it right out in the open. Even if I'm feeling completely disgusted with myself on the inside while I'm chewing, I've just never felt the need to stash wrappers in the bottom of the trash can or eat in the dark. It's just out there. Like, just this past weekend, my brother came over to help me bleed the brakes on my project car, and I just ordered this massive amount of takeout right in front of him, and... well, anyway, I just don't really hide it.
Do you think your episodes of eating out of control are usually triggered by feeling emotional, such as stressed, anxious, or upset?

Yeah, doc, it's pretty much exactly like what I was just trying to explain a minute ago. I really don't think it's an emotional thing, at least not in the way you're asking. I know a lot of people probably do that, right? Like you see it on TV where somebody gets dumped or they have a terrible day at the office and they just dive into a massive tub of ice cream while crying on the couch. But that's just not how it plays out for me. 

Like I was saying with the whole good day, bad day thing... my emotions just don't seem to be the driver here. I mean, I can be totally ticked off because I spent three hours trying to drill out a snapped exhaust manifold stud—which is incredibly frustrating, let me tell you, especially when you're working in a tight wheel well and your arms are cramping up and you're getting rust flakes in your eyes—and I'll go home after all that stress and I won't even look twice at the fridge. I'll just shower, maybe watch some TV, and go to bed. 

But then I can have a totally normal Tuesday, no stress, no anxiety, just doing basic PMs—preventative maintenance, you know, oil changes, checking brake lines—on a couple of school buses, just joking around with the guys in the bay, feeling pretty decent about life. And then I walk in my door and suddenly I'm tearing through the pantry and eating everything in sight. 

So, yeah, to answer your question again, I really don't think me feeling upset or stressed or anxious is the trigger. If it is, it's buried so deep under the hood that I can't even see it. It just feels totally random to me, not emotional at all. My brain and my stomach just don't seem to be communicating about how I'm actually feeling that day.
Do you feel like you're eating an abnormally large amount of food during these episodes?

Oh, yeah. Yeah, absolutely. I mean, it’s definitely not a normal amount of food, not by a long shot. Like, the whole reason I'm even talking to you about this is because lately... well, I'll get off a super long shift at the garage, or maybe I've been up half the night studying for my ASE transit bus certifications—because you gotta keep testing for those if you want to move up the pay scale, and the electrical systems ones are a real headache to memorize—and I’ll just end up eating way, way more than I ever planned to. 

Like, I'll tell myself I'm just gonna grab a quick bite on the drive home, right? Just something to take the edge off because I'm starving. But then I pull up to the drive-thru speaker, and suddenly I’m ordering a massive, full fast-food meal. And I don't mean just a regular combo—I'm talking two double quarter-pounders, the biggest fries they have, a twenty-piece chicken nugget, maybe a large shake. And I'll eat all of that. 

But then the crazy part is, that’s not even the end of it. I get back to my duplex, and it’s like that massive fast-food order was just the appetizer. I'll walk in, drop my keys, and go straight for the kitchen. I’ll start ripping into snacks, like a whole family-size bag of tortilla chips or an entire sleeve of cookies. And then I’m opening the fridge and just pulling out whatever’s in there. Could be half a leftover pizza from three days ago, cold hot dogs, just eating slices of cheese right out of the plastic... whatever I can get my hands on. 

And I'm eating all of this in one single sitting. I don't stop. It's just a mountain of food. So, yeah, when you ask if it's an abnormally large amount... man, it's enough to feed three full-grown guys, and I'm just putting it all away by myself in the span of like an hour or two. It's way, way over the line of what anybody would call a normal dinner.
Do you usually feel guilty or criticize yourself after these episodes of eating out of control?

Guilty? I don't... I don't know if I'd say guilty. And I definitely don't sit around criticizing myself, if that's what you mean. I mean, like I mentioned earlier, while I'm actually in the middle of chewing everything, yeah, I might feel kind of disgusted by what I'm doing, but once the episode is actually over? Once the food is completely gone? I don't sit there in the aftermath calling myself a failure or beating myself up or anything. 

It's more like... well, it's almost like a switch flips and my brain just goes totally blank. You know how it is when you've been busting your knuckles all day, maybe fighting with a seized caliper on a heavy-duty rig for four hours, and you finally get the damn thing off? You don't sit there analyzing your life choices, you're just totally drained. That's kind of how I feel after I eat all that food. I'm just sitting there on my couch, usually with whatever I was watching on Netflix still playing in the background—lately I've been watching this documentary series about vintage car restorations, which is pretty cool, they do amazing work with old rusted-out sheet metal, but I always end up missing half of the episodes when this happens—and I'm just physically so stuffed and wiped out that my brain doesn't even have the energy to criticize me. 

My stomach is usually stretched so tight it actually hurts, kinda like when you over-torque a bolt and you can feel the metal stretching right before it snaps. So I might be stressing about the calories, like I said before, just trying to figure out the math of it all, but as far as sitting there feeling guilty or telling myself I'm a bad person? Nah, I haven't really noticed anything like that. I'm mostly just... I don't know, just numb and exhausted.
Do you experience any physical symptoms after eating, such as nausea or stomach pain, that are not related to the guilt or panic you mentioned?

Well, like I was just saying, my stomach definitely gets stretched out. I mean, physically, it's pretty rough. Nausea? Not exactly, I don't think I feel like I'm gonna throw up or anything like that. It's more just this really intense fullness, you know? Like, if you take a balloon and you just keep blowing air into it, past the point where it's supposed to stop, and the rubber gets all thin and shiny and you just know it's gonna pop if you breathe on it wrong? That's what my gut feels like. 

It's just this heavy, painful stretching sensation. Like I said before, it actually hurts. It's not a sharp pain, like if you stabbed yourself with a screwdriver—which I've done, by the way, slipped right off a hose clamp and went straight into my palm, bled like crazy, had to wrap it in a shop rag and keep working—but it's this dull, relentless ache right in the middle of my stomach. And it just sits there. I can't get comfortable on the couch, I can't lay on my side, I just have to kind of sit propped up and wait for it to pass. 

Sometimes it feels like the food is just sitting right at the top of my throat, you know? Not like heartburn, really, just... like there's literally no more room left in the tank. You ever try to top off a fuel tank on a big rig and you misjudge it, and the diesel just comes spilling right back up the filler neck and gets all over your boots? It's kind of like that feeling, just completely topped out. So yeah, I guess you could say stomach pain is a big part of it, just from sheer volume, but not really nausea in the traditional sense. Just... incredibly, painfully full.
Do you ever try to compensate for the amount of food you eat during these episodes by fasting or severely restricting your food intake on the following days?

Yeah, I mean, I definitely try to make up for it. Like, after a really bad night of eating—when I’ve just completely overdone it and I wake up feeling like garbage—I’ll just tell myself, 'Alright, that’s it, nothing goes in the tank today.' So I'll just skip breakfast entirely. 

And then I get to the garage, and I’ll skip lunch, too. The other guys at the shop, they always take a break around noon, usually grabbing something from the roach coach that rolls by, or maybe ordering meatball subs from this Italian place down the street. And man, it smells amazing when they bring it into the breakroom, but I just sit there drinking black coffee or water and I just keep working. I'll tell them I'm not hungry or I want to finish up a job, and I just push right through the whole shift on an empty stomach. 

But it’s not just the skipping meals part, either. I’ll actually try to physically burn it all off. Like, I’ll force myself to go for these extra long runs, or I’ll drop down in my living room and just do sets of push-ups until my arms are shaking and I literally can't push myself off the floor anymore. And the crazy thing is, I’m already completely worn out. Being a diesel mechanic, you’re on your feet all day, ten or twelve hours sometimes, hauling heavy tools around, wrestling with transmissions and heavy-duty axles. It's not a desk job, you know? It takes a toll on your body. So I'm already physically exhausted by the time I clock out. 

But I just... I don't know, I feel like I have to push myself through those extra runs and push-ups anyway. Even when my legs feel like lead and my shoulders are screaming at me from wrenching all day, I just force myself to do it, just to try and undo all the damage from the night before, you know? It's like I have to balance the math out somehow, no matter how tired I am.
Do you think these episodes of eating out of control are related to your attempts to restrict food intake on other days?

I mean... I don't know, honestly. I haven't really thought about it like that, like one causing the other. It's more like... well, it's just this cycle I get stuck in, you know? I restrict and I run myself ragged because I ate too much, not the other way around. At least, that's how it feels in my head. 

But I guess... I mean, if I really stop and think about it... when I'm going all day on just black coffee and fumes, by the time I get home, I'm just ravenous. I'll walk through the door and my stomach is just growling so loud you could hear it over a running Cummins engine, and I'm just so depleted. You know, you spend all day under a chassis, dealing with grease and dirt and stripped bolts, and you're just physically and mentally drained. And then you haven't eaten a single thing since the night before. So yeah, maybe by the time evening rolls around, I'm just so hungry that once I start eating, I just can't hit the brakes. 

But I don't know if I'd say the restricting *causes* the out-of-control eating. It's more like... I have to restrict because of what I did, and then... well, I guess then I do it again. It's like trying to fix a blown head gasket by just pouring more coolant in, you know? You're not fixing the problem, you're just dealing with the symptom, and eventually the whole thing is gonna overheat again. But I just don't know how else to handle it. I don't really sit there analyzing the connection, I'm just trying to survive the day and keep my weight from spiraling out of control. So, I don't know. Maybe they are connected, but I haven't really noticed it working like that.
Have these episodes of eating out of control affected your relationships with family or friends, or impacted your ability to work or perform daily activities?

Yeah, I mean... I’m still getting to the shop every day, you know? I haven't missed a shift or called out sick or anything like that. I pride myself on being reliable, showing up when I'm supposed to. But... man, it's definitely taking a toll. I'm just so worn down during my shifts lately. When you're wrenching on a 15-ton rig, you really need your head in the game. Like, if you torque a bolt wrong on an air brake system, or you lose focus while you're under a suspended axle, that's not just a little mistake, that's incredibly dangerous. You could get yourself or someone else seriously hurt. 

And honestly, I'm just... I'm really distracted. I'll be staring at a schematic for a transmission, or trying to trace a wiring fault, and my brain is just completely foggy. I'm physically there, my hands are dirty and I'm turning the wrenches, but my mind is just spinning about the night before, or how heavy my legs feel from working out, or what I'm going to do about dinner when I get home. It’s like running an engine with the timing all messed up—it’s running, sure, but it’s running rough, and you can feel it shaking the whole chassis. It just takes twice the effort to get through a standard twelve-hour shift now.

And as for the guys at work... yeah, it's affecting that, too. Like I was saying earlier about lunchtime? I completely avoid eating with the other mechanics now. We used to all sit around in the breakroom, bust each other's chops, talk about trucks or whatever the game was last night... but I just can't do it anymore. I don't want anyone noticing my eating habits. Mechanics are observant guys, you know? They notice when a part looks wrong, and they notice when a guy is acting weird. If I sit there and eat with them, I'm terrified they're gonna see how anxious I get around the food, or I'll end up eating too much and they'll look at me funny. Or if I sit there with just my black coffee every single day, they're gonna start asking questions I don't want to answer. 

So I just isolate myself. I tell them I've got to finish a tear-down in bay three, or I just go sit out in my own truck in the parking lot with the radio on. It sucks, because I like those guys, they're my buddies, but I just... I can't let them see how weird I get about eating. So I just keep my head down and stay away from them.
Do you think your attempts to compensate for the food you eat, such as through excessive exercise or fasting, are an attempt to prevent weight gain?

Oh, yeah, one hundred percent. I mean, that's exactly what it is. It's all about the weight. Because, look, if I didn't do all that... if I just ate the way I do on those really bad nights and then just went about a normal day without trying to fix it? Man, I’d blow up like a balloon. I can't even imagine what the scale would say. 

And in my line of work, you really can't afford to be carrying around a bunch of extra dead weight. Like, I’m crawling under these massive rigs, squeezing between axles and fuel tanks, contorting my body just to get a wrench on a bolt that some engineer decided to hide in the worst possible spot. If I get big, if I let myself gain all that weight from eating like that, I literally wouldn't fit under half the chassis I work on. 

So yeah, like I was saying before, after a bad night of eating, I’ll just completely skip breakfast and lunch at work. I just won't let myself have anything. Or I'll force myself to push through those extra long runs and do sets of push-ups in my living room, even when I’m completely worn out from being on my feet all day. I mean, I'm already exhausted, my back aches, my hands are cramped up from gripping tools for twelve hours, but in my head, all I can see is that food turning into fat, you know? 

It's like this panic just sets in. I start calculating everything from the night before, thinking about how many pounds that's gonna translate to if I don't burn it off or starve it off immediately. So I just keep running, or I just keep fasting the next day, because the thought of stepping on the scale and seeing it shoot up... it just terrifies me. I just can't let myself get fat. I have to keep the weight off, no matter how much it hurts to do those extra workouts when my body is just screaming for a break.
Do you ever feel like you are eating in response to an emotional state, such as sadness, anxiety, or boredom?

I mean, honestly... no. I really don't think it's an emotional thing. Like, you mentioned boredom? Man, I wish I had the time to be bored. When you're working in a heavy-duty diesel shop, there is zero downtime. You're constantly moving, pulling transmissions, dealing with service managers breathing down your neck about turnaround times... there's no sitting around twiddling your thumbs. I'm exhausted, not bored. 

And sadness? I don't know, I wouldn't say I'm sad. I'm not really a depressed guy, you know? I'm just a guy trying to get through the week and pay my bills. As for anxiety... I mean, sure, I get anxious about my weight, like I just told you, but I don't eat *because* I'm anxious. If anything, being anxious about getting fat makes me want to avoid food entirely. 

When I have those nights where I just lose control and eat everything in sight, it doesn't feel like I'm trying to comfort myself or, like, eat my feelings. It really just feels purely physical. Like I was saying before about the fasting and surviving on black coffee... by the time I get home, my tank is just completely on empty. It’s not a mood thing at all. My body is just screaming for fuel because I've been burning it all day hauling heavy parts around, wrestling with tires that weigh more than I do, and I haven't given my body a single thing to run on. 

So, no, I don't sit on the couch crying into a box of pizza or anything like that. I'm just starving. It's like... if you run a diesel engine without oil, it's going to seize up. It's not because the engine is sad or stressed, it's just physics. It's a mechanical failure. That's exactly how my stomach feels. It's just empty, and the hunger just takes over my brain. So yeah, I really haven't noticed it being tied to my emotions at all. I don't really sit around analyzing my feelings anyway. It's just... I'm hungry because I didn't eat, and then I start eating and I can't stop, and then I have to fix it the next day so I don't blow up. That's really all it is, just that same physical cycle over and over.
Do you think your eating out of control is ever triggered by feelings of sadness?

Like I was just saying a second ago, no, not at all. Sadness really doesn't have anything to do with it. I mean, I know people do that, right? You see it on TV or whatever, someone gets their heart broken or they're crying about something and they just sit on the couch with a whole gallon of ice cream. But that's just not me. I don't really get sad like that anyway. 

I mean, sure, I get frustrated. Like, if I'm working on a Peterbilt and I snap a rusted bolt flush with the engine block and I know I'm gonna have to spend the next three hours drilling and tapping it just to salvage the job... yeah, I'm ticked off. I'll throw a wrench across the shop. But sad? Not really. And honestly, even if I was sad about something, it doesn't make me want to eat. If anything, when I'm actually upset about something, my stomach just ties up in knots and I don't even want to look at food. 

But these nights where I just eat and eat and can't stop... it's not because I had a bad day emotionally or because I'm feeling sorry for myself. It's literally just because I haven't eaten a single thing all day. My body is just completely drained. You gotta understand, I'm lifting heavy parts, swinging hammers, dragging myself around on creepers, and wrestling with dual tires all day long. By the time I clock out, I'm physically shaking because my tank is just completely zeroed out. 

So when I get home and tear through the kitchen, it's not a sadness thing, it's a survival thing. My brain is just screaming for calories. I don't want you to think there's some hidden emotional trauma or that I'm secretly crying in the cab of my truck, because I'm really not. It's just the mechanics of it, plain and simple. I starve myself all day because I'm terrified of getting fat, and then the fuel runs out, and my body just takes over. That's really all it boils down to.
Do you think your episodes of eating out of control are usually triggered by a specific emotional state, such as feeling overwhelmed or frustrated?

I feel like we're kind of going in circles here, Doc. Like I was just saying about getting frustrated... no. It really doesn't trigger the eating.

I starve myself, I work my butt off all day hauling heavy metal around, and then my brain just forces me to eat because my tank is completely empty. That's all it is.

Well, yeah. I mean, absolutely. That's the whole reason I don't eat during the day, right? Because I am just completely terrified of getting bigger. It's like this constant loop in my head.

I drink my black coffee, I drive to the shop, I bust my knuckles all day, and I'm just running on pure panic about that one stupid pound. 

And then, because I did that... because I let that number on the scale scare me into starving myself for fourteen hours straight while I'm doing manual labor... that's exactly why I end up coming home and eating everything in the kitchen. So yeah, the fear of gaining weight is definitely what starts the whole domino effect. If I wasn't so paranoid about it, maybe I'd actually eat a normal sandwich at lunch like the other guys in the bay instead of setting myself up to crash and burn every night. But I just can't bring myself to do it. The second I think about eating during the day, I just picture that scale going up, and I panic. It's like I have to balance the math out somehow, no matter how tired I am.

doctor.question: Do you think these episodes of eating out of control are related to your attempts to restrict food intake on other days?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the causal relationship between the patient's dietary restriction and binge eating episodes, which is not a specific diagnostic criterion listed in the symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I mean... I don't know, honestly. I haven't really thought about it like that, like one causing the other. It's more like... well, it's just this cycle I get stuck in, you know? I restrict and I run myself ragged because I ate too much, not the other way around. At least, that's how it feels in my head. 

But I guess... I mean, if I really stop and think about it... when I'm going all day on just black coffee and fumes, by the time I get home, I'm just ravenous. I'll walk through the door and my stomach is just growling so loud you could hear it over a running Cummins engine, and I'm just so depleted. You know, you spend all day under a chassis, dealing with grease and dirt and stripped bolts, and you're just physically and mentally drained. And then you haven't eaten a single thing since the night before. So yeah, maybe by the time evening rolls around, I'm just so hungry that once I start eating, I just can't hit the brakes. 

But I don't know if I'd say the restricting *causes* the out-of-control eating. It's more like... I have to restrict because of what I did, and then... well, I guess then I do it again. It's like trying to fix a blown head gasket by just pouring more coolant in, you know? You're not fixing the problem, you're just dealing with the symptom, and eventually the whole thing is gonna overheat again. But I just don't know how else to handle it. I don't really sit there analyzing the connection, I'm just trying to survive the day and keep my weight from spiraling out of control. So, I don't know. Maybe they are connected, but I haven't really noticed it working like that.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's episodes of eating out of control are significantly impacting their daily life and relationships
doctor.question: Have these episodes of eating out of control affected your relationships with family or friends, or impacted your ability to work or perform daily activities?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still getting to the shop, but I’m more distracted and worn down during shifts, and I avoid lunch with the other mechanics because I don’t want anyone noticing my eating habits.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about how the symptoms have affected my relationships, work, or daily activities, which directly maps to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I mean... I’m still getting to the shop every day, you know? I haven't missed a shift or called out sick or anything like that. I pride myself on being reliable, showing up when I'm supposed to. But... man, it's definitely taking a toll. I'm just so worn down during my shifts lately. When you're wrenching on a 15-ton rig, you really need your head in the game. Like, if you torque a bolt wrong on an air brake system, or you lose focus while you're under a suspended axle, that's not just a little mistake, that's incredibly dangerous. You could get yourself or someone else seriously hurt. 

And honestly, I'm just... I'm really distracted. I'll be staring at a schematic for a transmission, or trying to trace a wiring fault, and my brain is just completely foggy. I'm physically there, my hands are dirty and I'm turning the wrenches, but my mind is just spinning about the night before, or how heavy my legs feel from working out, or what I'm going to do about dinner when I get home. It’s like running an engine with the timing all messed up—it’s running, sure, but it’s running rough, and you can feel it shaking the whole chassis. It just takes twice the effort to get through a standard twelve-hour shift now.

And as for the guys at work... yeah, it's affecting that, too. Like I was saying earlier about lunchtime? I completely avoid eating with the other mechanics now. We used to all sit around in the breakroom, bust each other's chops, talk about trucks or whatever the game was last night... but I just can't do it anymore. I don't want anyone noticing my eating habits. Mechanics are observant guys, you know? They notice when a part looks wrong, and they notice when a guy is acting weird. If I sit there and eat with them, I'm terrified they're gonna see how anxious I get around the food, or I'll end up eating too much and they'll look at me funny. Or if I sit there with just my black coffee every single day, they're gonna start asking questions I don't want to answer. 

So I just isolate myself. I tell them I've got to finish a tear-down in bay three, or I just go sit out in my own truck in the parking lot with the radio on. It sucks, because I like those guys, they're my buddies, but I just... I can't let them see how weird I get about eating. So I just keep my head down and stay away from them.

doctor.intent: Determine if patient's behavior is more aligned with binge eating disorder or other eating disorders
doctor.question: Do you think your attempts to compensate for the food you eat, such as through excessive exercise or fasting, are an attempt to prevent weight gain?

target_item.name: Compensatory_Behavior_NonPurging
target_item.manifestation: After a bad night of eating, I’ll skip breakfast and lunch at work or push myself through extra runs and push-ups even when I’m worn out from being on my feet all day.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the compensatory behaviors previously discussed (excessive exercise, fasting) are intended to prevent weight gain, which directly aligns with the definition of Compensatory_Behavior_NonPurging.

patient.answer:
Oh, yeah, one hundred percent. I mean, that's exactly what it is. It's all about the weight. Because, look, if I didn't do all that... if I just ate the way I do on those really bad nights and then just went about a normal day without trying to fix it? Man, I’d blow up like a balloon. I can't even imagine what the scale would say. 

And in my line of work, you really can't afford to be carrying around a bunch of extra dead weight. Like, I’m crawling under these massive rigs, squeezing between axles and fuel tanks, contorting my body just to get a wrench on a bolt that some engineer decided to hide in the worst possible spot. If I get big, if I let myself gain all that weight from eating like that, I literally wouldn't fit under half the chassis I work on. 

So yeah, like I was saying before, after a bad night of eating, I’ll just completely skip breakfast and lunch at work. I just won't let myself have anything. Or I'll force myself to push through those extra long runs and do sets of push-ups in my living room, even when I’m completely worn out from being on my feet all day. I mean, I'm already exhausted, my back aches, my hands are cramped up from gripping tools for twelve hours, but in my head, all I can see is that food turning into fat, you know? 

It's like this panic just sets in. I start calculating everything from the night before, thinking about how many pounds that's gonna translate to if I don't burn it off or starve it off immediately. So I just keep running, or I just keep fasting the next day, because the thought of stepping on the scale and seeing it shoot up... it just terrifies me. I just can't let myself get fat. I have to keep the weight off, no matter how much it hurts to do those extra workouts when my body is just screaming for a break.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is more aligned with binge eating disorder or other eating disorders
doctor.question: Do you ever feel like you are eating in response to an emotional state, such as sadness, anxiety, or boredom?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about emotional triggers for eating episodes (e.g., sadness, anxiety, boredom), which is not a specific diagnostic criterion in the provided symptom profile for Bulimia Nervosa.

patient.answer:
I mean, honestly... no. I really don't think it's an emotional thing. Like, you mentioned boredom? Man, I wish I had the time to be bored. When you're working in a heavy-duty diesel shop, there is zero downtime. You're constantly moving, pulling transmissions, dealing with service managers breathing down your neck about turnaround times... there's no sitting around twiddling your thumbs. I'm exhausted, not bored. 

And sadness? I don't know, I wouldn't say I'm sad. I'm not really a depressed guy, you know? I'm just a guy trying to get through the week and pay my bills. As for anxiety... I mean, sure, I get anxious about my weight, like I just told you, but I don't eat *because* I'm anxious. If anything, being anxious about getting fat makes me want to avoid food entirely. 

When I have those nights where I just lose control and eat everything in sight, it doesn't feel like I'm trying to comfort myself or, like, eat my feelings. It really just feels purely physical. Like I was saying before about the fasting and surviving on black coffee... by the time I get home, my tank is just completely on empty. It’s not a mood thing at all. My body is just screaming for fuel because I've been burning it all day hauling heavy parts around, wrestling with tires that weigh more than I do, and I haven't given my body a single thing to run on. 

So, no, I don't sit on the couch crying into a box of pizza or anything like that. I'm just starving. It's like... if you run a diesel engine without oil, it's going to seize up. It's not because the engine is sad or stressed, it's just physics. It's a mechanical failure. That's exactly how my stomach feels. It's just empty, and the hunger just takes over my brain. So yeah, I really haven't noticed it being tied to my emotions at all. I don't really sit around analyzing my feelings anyway. It's just... I'm hungry because I didn't eat, and then I start eating and I can't stop, and then I have to fix it the next day so I don't blow up. That's really all it is, just that same physical cycle over and over.

doctor.intent: Determine if patient's eating behavior is driven by emotional states
doctor.question: Do you think your eating out of control is ever triggered by feelings of sadness?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if my out-of-control eating is triggered by sadness, which explores emotional triggers for binge eating. This is not covered by my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Like I was just saying a second ago, no, not at all. Sadness really doesn't have anything to do with it. I mean, I know people do that, right? You see it on TV or whatever, someone gets their heart broken or they're crying about something and they just sit on the couch with a whole gallon of ice cream. But that's just not me. I don't really get sad like that anyway. 

I mean, sure, I get frustrated. Like, if I'm working on a Peterbilt and I snap a rusted bolt flush with the engine block and I know I'm gonna have to spend the next three hours drilling and tapping it just to salvage the job... yeah, I'm ticked off. I'll throw a wrench across the shop. But sad? Not really. And honestly, even if I was sad about something, it doesn't make me want to eat. If anything, when I'm actually upset about something, my stomach just ties up in knots and I don't even want to look at food. 

But these nights where I just eat and eat and can't stop... it's not because I had a bad day emotionally or because I'm feeling sorry for myself. It's literally just because I haven't eaten a single thing all day. My body is just completely drained. You gotta understand, I'm lifting heavy parts, swinging hammers, dragging myself around on creepers, and wrestling with dual tires all day long. By the time I clock out, I'm physically shaking because my tank is just completely zeroed out. 

So when I get home and tear through the kitchen, it's not a sadness thing, it's a survival thing. My brain is just screaming for calories. I don't want you to think there's some hidden emotional trauma or that I'm secretly crying in the cab of my truck, because I'm really not. It's just the mechanics of it, plain and simple. I starve myself all day because I'm terrified of getting fat, and then the fuel runs out, and my body just takes over. That's really all it boils down to.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's eating behavior is related to a specific emotional state
doctor.question: Do you think your episodes of eating out of control are usually triggered by a specific emotional state, such as feeling overwhelmed or frustrated?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about specific emotional triggers (feeling overwhelmed or frustrated) for the binge eating episodes. While the symptom profile covers binge eating and loss of control, it does not specifically include emotional triggers as a separate symptom criteria to be evaluated.

patient.answer:
I feel like we're kind of going in circles here, Doc. Like I was just saying about getting frustrated... no. It really doesn't trigger the eating. 

I mean, sure, I get overwhelmed. You try working in a bay when it's ninety degrees out and you've got three different service managers barking at you about turnaround times. Just yesterday, I had this absolute nightmare of a job on a Freightliner. The guy comes out and tells me I need to have a transmission pulled and swapped by the end of my shift, and I'm under there, covered in grease, sweating through my coveralls, and every single bolt on the bell housing is seized up tight. I'm hitting it with the impact gun, soaking it in penetrant, heating it up with the torch... and nothing. I was so overwhelmed and ticked off I thought I was gonna blow a gasket right there on the shop floor. 

But when that happens? When I'm in the thick of it and just completely stressed out? Eating is the absolute last thing on my mind. My stomach gets all tight, you know? Like a clenched fist. If someone handed me a sandwich right then, I'd probably throw it at the wall. I just get mad. I don't get hungry. 

So, no, it's not the frustration. By the time I actually get home and start tearing through the cupboards, the frustration from the shop is long gone. I'm just tired. And I'm starving. Because, like I keep trying to explain, I haven't eaten a single thing since the night before because I'm so paranoid about gaining weight and not fitting under the trucks. It's just my body giving out on me. It's not some deep emotional reaction to having a tough day at work or feeling overwhelmed by a job. I really don't know how else to say it, it's just... I starve myself, I work my butt off all day hauling heavy metal around, and then my brain just forces me to eat because my tank is completely empty. That's all it is.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's eating out of control is related to a fear of gaining weight
doctor.question: Do you think your fear of gaining weight directly contributes to your episodes of eating out of control?

target_item.name: Fear_of_Weight_Gain
target_item.manifestation: Even when my work pants are looser, if the scale is up even a pound I feel like I’m getting fat and I start worrying I’m going to lose control of my whole body.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking directly about my fear of gaining weight and how it relates to my eating behaviors.

patient.answer:
Well, yeah. I mean, absolutely. That's the whole reason I don't eat during the day, right? Because I am just completely terrified of getting bigger. It's like this constant loop in my head. 

I weigh myself every single morning, first thing, before I even jump in the shower. It's a whole ritual, and honestly, it just completely dictates my entire day. It messes with my head so bad. Like, I could get dressed for the shop, put on my heavy-duty work pants, and I can physically feel that they're bagging on me. I'll have to pull my belt a notch tighter just to keep them up while I'm working. So logically, I know I've shrunk. I know I'm smaller. But even when my work pants are noticeably looser like that, if I step on that scale and it is up even a single pound from the day before... man, it just ruins me. I instantly feel like I’m getting fat. My brain just spirals, and I start worrying that I’m going to completely lose control of my whole body. 

It's like, I see that number go up by one pound, or even half a pound, and suddenly I'm convinced I'm gonna balloon up and not be able to slide on a creeper under a chassis anymore. So then I tell myself, "Okay, that's it, you can't have anything today. Not a single calorie." I drink my black coffee, I drive to the shop, I bust my knuckles all day, and I'm just running on pure panic about that one stupid pound. 

And then, because I did that... because I let that number on the scale scare me into starving myself for fourteen hours straight while I'm doing manual labor... that's exactly why I end up coming home and eating everything in the kitchen. So yeah, the fear of gaining weight is definitely what starts the whole domino effect. If I wasn't so paranoid about it, maybe I'd actually eat a normal sandwich at lunch like the other guys in the bay instead of setting myself up to crash and burn every night. But I just can't bring myself to do it. The second I think about eating during the day, I just picture that scale going up, and I panic. I just can't handle the idea of losing control of my size, even though, ironically, it makes me lose control of my eating later on. It's messed up, I know, but that's exactly how it happens.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms of recurrent episodes of eating out of control, followed by compensatory behaviors such as fasting, excessive exercise, and purging, are consistent with bulimia nervosa. The patient's fear of gaining weight and self-evaluation being unduly influenced by body weight or shape also support this diagnosis.
